content.text: In this trace the gap sits between the caller's client span and the callee's server span. For example, route-plan's POST to travel2 took 3418 ms on the client side but only 6.7 ms on the server side, so the delay is on the connection or in the caller's HTTP layer, not in the callee. I'll check the per-connection hubble HTTP latency to see which connections carry that delay.

input.query: SELECT metric, attr_source, attr_destination, COUNT(*) n FROM normal_metrics_sum WHERE metric LIKE 'hubble%' GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 20

content.text: Hubble exposes per-pair HTTP duration. I'll compare its p95 per connection between periods, limited to the services on the failing path.

input.query: SELECT 'N' p, metric, attr_source, attr_destination, COUNT(*) n FROM normal_metrics_histogram GROUP BY ALL LIMIT 3

SELECT metric, attr_source src, attr_destination dst, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p='N' THEN sum END)/NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN p='N' THEN count END),0)*1000,2) meanN_ms, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p='A' THEN sum END)/NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN p='A' THEN count END),0)*1000,2) meanA_ms, SUM(CASE WHEN p='N' THEN count END) cN, SUM(CASE WHEN p='A' THEN count END) cA FROM (SELECT 'N' p,* FROM normal_metrics_histogram UNION ALL SELECT 'A' p,* FROM abnormal_metrics_histogram) WHERE metric='hubble_http_request_duration_seconds' AND attr_source IS NOT NULL AND attr_destination IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ALL HAVING cA>0 AND cN>0 ORDER BY (meanA_ms/meanN_ms) DESC LIMIT 25

content.text: Hubble histogram values are mostly sub-millisecond and don't show a clear shift, so I'll drop that line. Instead I'll match each client span to its server child by parent ID and measure the gap by caller service, comparing periods.

input.query: WITH cs AS (SELECT p, span_id, service_name caller, duration d FROM (SELECT 'N' p,* FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'A' p,* FROM abnormal_traces) WHERE attr_span_kind='Client'), ss AS (SELECT p, parent_span_id, service_name callee, duration d FROM (SELECT 'N' p,* FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'A' p,* FROM abnormal_traces) WHERE attr_span_kind='Server') SELECT cs.caller, ss.callee, COUNT(*) pairs_N_A, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN cs.p='N' THEN (cs.d-ss.d)/1e6 END),2) gapN_ms, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN cs.p='A' THEN (cs.d-ss.d)/1e6 END),2) gapA_ms, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN cs.p='N' THEN ss.d/1e6 END),2) calleeN_ms, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN cs.p='A' THEN ss.d/1e6 END),2) calleeA_ms FROM cs JOIN ss ON cs.span_id = ss.parent_span_id AND cs.p=ss.p GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING COUNT(*)>30 ORDER BY (gapA_ms-gapN_ms) DESC LIMIT 30

content.text: The largest connection-level gaps are route-plan→route-service, travel→basic, and security→order. Before drawing conclusions I want to rule out restarts. I'll check restart counters and pod-level metric changes in the abnormal window.

input.query: SELECT 'A' p, metric, service_name, attr_k8s_pod_name pod, MIN(value) mn, MAX(value) mx, COUNT(*) n FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE metric IN ('k8s.container.restarts','k8s.container.ready','k8s.pod.phase') GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'N', metric, service_name, attr_k8s_pod_name, MIN(value), MAX(value), COUNT(*) FROM normal_metrics WHERE metric IN ('k8s.container.restarts','k8s.container.ready') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,3,1 LIMIT 60

content.text: No pod restarted and all containers stayed ready, so this is not a lifecycle fault. The gap appears after the callee has already responded. To separate per-path HTTP faults from connection-level faults, I'll break the gap down by caller, callee, and path.

input.query: WITH cs AS (SELECT p, span_id, service_name caller, attr_k8s_pod_name cpod, CAST(duration AS DOUBLE) d FROM (SELECT 'N' p,* FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'A' p,* FROM abnormal_traces) WHERE attr_span_kind='Client'), ss AS (SELECT p, parent_span_id, service_name callee, span_name sn, CAST(duration AS DOUBLE) d FROM (SELECT 'N' p,* FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'A' p,* FROM abnormal_traces) WHERE attr_span_kind='Server') SELECT cs.caller, cs.cpod, ss.callee, ss.sn, SUM(CASE WHEN cs.p='N' THEN 1 END) nN, SUM(CASE WHEN cs.p='A' THEN 1 END) nA, ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN cs.p='N' THEN (cs.d-ss.d) END,0.5)/1e6,1) medGapN, ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN cs.p='A' THEN (cs.d-ss.d) END,0.5)/1e6,1) medGapA, ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN cs.p='A' THEN (cs.d-ss.d) END,0.9)/1e6,1) p90GapA FROM cs JOIN ss ON cs.span_id = ss.parent_span_id AND cs.p=ss.p WHERE cs.caller IN ('ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-service','ts-basic-service','ts-security-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-travel-plan-service') GROUP BY ALL HAVING nA>=20 ORDER BY medGapA DESC LIMIT 30

content.text: Median gaps are essentially unchanged, so the effect is in the tail only. The trace also shows about 2.9 s of time inside route-plan's `getMinStopStations` with no child spans. I'll compute self-time (span duration minus direct children) for internal methods to find where that time sits.

input.query: WITH all_s AS (SELECT 'N' p, * FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'A' p, * FROM abnormal_traces), ch AS (SELECT p, parent_span_id, SUM(CAST(duration AS DOUBLE)) cd, COUNT(*) nc FROM all_s GROUP BY 1,2), selfT AS (SELECT s.p, s.service_name svc, s.span_name, CAST(s.duration AS DOUBLE) - COALESCE(ch.cd,0) self_d FROM all_s s LEFT JOIN ch ON ch.p=s.p AND ch.parent_span_id=s.span_id WHERE s.attr_span_kind='Internal' AND s.service_name IN ('ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-travel-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-basic-service','ts-route-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-food-service','ts-security-service','ts-seat-service','ts-ui-dashboard')) SELECT svc, span_name, SUM(CASE WHEN p='N' THEN 1 END) nN, SUM(CASE WHEN p='A' THEN 1 END) nA, ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN p='N' THEN self_d END,0.5)/1e6,2) selfMedN, ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN p='A' THEN self_d END,0.5)/1e6,2) selfMedA, ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN p='N' THEN self_d END,0.95)/1e6,2) selfP95N, ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN p='A' THEN self_d END,0.95)/1e6,2) selfP95A FROM selfT GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING nA>=30 ORDER BY selfP95A DESC LIMIT 25

content.text: Self-times are mostly flat, with changes only in the tail. Route-service's repository methods and preserve's own method both show p95 jumps but unchanged medians. content.text: The only other restart counter, on ticket-office-service, is flat across the window, so it isn't a fault here. Next I'll check whether the caller-side gap to route-service grows minute by minute, to tell a connection-level delay from in-process slowness at route-service.

input.query: WITH cs AS (SELECT span_id, time, service_name caller, CAST(duration AS DOUBLE) d FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Client'), ss AS (SELECT parent_span_id, service_name callee, span_name sn, CAST(duration AS DOUBLE) d FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Server' AND service_name='ts-route-service') SELECT date_trunc('minute', cs.time) m, cs.caller, COUNT(*) n, ROUND(quantile_cont(cs.d-ss.d,0.5)/1e6,1) medGap, ROUND(quantile_cont(cs.d-ss.d,0.9)/1e6,1) p90Gap, ROUND(quantile_cont(ss.d,0.5)/1e6,1) medSrv FROM cs JOIN ss ON cs.span_id=ss.parent_span_id GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 2,1

**Verdict: the evidence supports `pod_failure` for `ts-preserve-service`. Confidence is moderate-high.** The equivalence class also covers `pod_unavailable`, and the telemetry shows the pod came back, so `pod_failure` is the better member.

**What supports it**
- **Container restart, same pod:** `k8s.container.restarts` for `ts-preserve-service-5d979f4b55-n6ccw` was 0 in the normal window and reads 1 from 01:21:36 to 01:25:26. The pod name did not change, so the container restarted in place.
- **Brief gap, then recovery:** preserve's Server spans are absent until 01:22:07, and its INFO logs start at 01:21:58. Its metrics keep arriving through 01:25, so the pod was not gone for the rest of the window.
- **No resource build-up before the restart:** `container.cpu.usage` is 0.0 at 01:21:34, just before the restart. The first post-restart samples show start-up CPU (1.63 at 01:21:39) and memory around 295 MB, which fits a fresh process rather than saturation.
- **Callers refused, then recovered:** all 17 dashboard 503s on the preserve route fall between 01:21:31 and 01:22:06. Each takes about 3.5 s, and there are no 503s after that. Successful calls return from 01:21:49 onward, with some still failing in between.

**Evidence against or complicating it**
- **Timing of the first failure:** the first dashboard 503 is at 01:21:31, about five seconds before the restart counter first reads 1 at 01:21:36. Counter sampling could explain this, but the restart may have begun earlier than the counter shows.
- **Readiness does not show the gap:** `k8s.container.ready` reads 1.0 in every sample, so it does not confirm the outage. The gap rests on the span and log silence.
- **Cause of the restart is not established:** the abnormal window has almost no preserve metrics before 01:21:34, so I cannot rule out an earlier cause.
- **Outbound tail is not explained by the restart:** preserve's calls to every callee show a p95 rise with a flat median, which is a tail pattern. Its own Client spans also worsen through 01:24–01:25 (p50 14→40→90 ms, p95 83→457→1,448 ms), although call volume falls and the mix shifts, so the cause is unclear. This could be cold-JVM and new-connection effects after the restart, or a separate network effect on preserve's outbound links. The hubble drops are 0, so I found no direct sign of network loss. This does not change the pod-restart finding, but it means the incident may include a second effect that this claim does not cover.

**Alternatives considered**
- **`network_partition` at the dashboard→preserve link:** unlikely. Preserve stayed alive and logging, the hubble flows on that link rose (110→340 per minute) with no drops, and a partition would not produce a container restart counter or a recovery within about 25 seconds.
- **`http_aborted`:** the 503s take about 3.5 s, not about 1 ms, and the dashboard log text does not show an aborted response. I did not find the upstream error text, so this is not ruled out by the logs.
- **CPU, memory or JVM saturation:** the pre-restart CPU is near zero, and the memory evidence reflects start-up, not saturation.
- **`dns_lookup_failed`:** no name-resolution errors appeared in the logs I checked.

**Verdict: the evidence does not support `database_call_slow` for `ts-route-service`.** The database statements themselves did not slow. The lead's three signals are real but point to a process-level stall, not a slow database.

**What the data shows**

- **The statements are flat.** The client-side SQL spans barely moved: `SELECT ts.route` p50 0.42 → 0.43 ms and p95 0.76 → 1.23 ms; `SELECT ts.route_stations` and `SELECT ts.route_distances` p50 are unchanged at 0.28 and 0.27 ms. A `database_call_slow` fault would show these statement durations growing by a steady amount. They do not.
- **The growth sits around the DB calls, not in them.** `RouteRepository.findById` median is about 2 ms through 01:24 and only jumps at 01:25 (12.8 ms, n=35). Its SQL child is still about 0.5–1 ms. The extra time is spent in the gap around the statement.
- **The pool wait is spiky and the pool is not saturated.** Mean wait per minute is 45, 31, 48 ms for 01:22–01:24, then 1,451 ms at 01:25. Over the same window the pool shows `max` 10, `usage` 5 and `pending_requests` 0. Connections were available and nothing was queued. A slow database would not produce this shape.
- **The 01:25 spike lines up with a GC pause.** `jvm.gc.duration` shows one collection of 2,370 ms in that minute, and the pool-wait and findById spikes happen in the same minute. A process-wide stall that holds threads before they reach the connection would produce exactly this, so the lead's `Transaction.commit` tail is probably the same stall too.
- **The tail shape is not a network fault either.** Route-service's own Server spans show p50 flat and p95 up (`GET /routes` p95 14 → 60 ms, p50 10.8 → 10.9 ms). That is a tail-only shift, but it is inside the service, not on a connection.
- **The whole system lost load.** Calls per minute fell by about 35% on nearly every route, including callers that do not depend on route-service's database. The slowdown is not specific to route-service's DB path.

**Alternatives I checked and set aside**

- `network_delay` or a network fault to MySQL: the statement spans would be slower and the spread would widen. Neither happens, and there are no DB connection errors.
- `container_memory_saturated` or `jvm_heap_exhausted`: JVM heap use is about 46–61 MB across the window, with no ramp toward a limit.
- `container_cpu_saturated`: not checked in this pass.

**Confidence and limits**

- `database_call_slow` for route-service: **low**. The statement-level evidence contradicts it.
- The closest candidate is `jvm_gc_thrashing`, with **low to moderate** confidence. The support is one 2.4 s pause at 01:25 that coincides with the wait-time and findById spikes. Against it: normal-period GC already averages about 319 ms per collection, and heap is not near any limit.
- The abnormal metrics cover only about four minutes, so one pause is thin evidence. A stronger check would be the per-pause GC series and route-service's container CPU across the window.
